catalog_citation: Jonker, J.C.G. 1915. Rottineesche spraakkunst. Leiden: E.J. Brill. (pp. 5-6)
catalog_quote: § 4. Het accent, dat in het Rottineesch duidelijk hoorbaar is, valt bij een twee-lettergrepig stamwoord of bij de afleidingen daarvan, als ook op de drie-lettergrepige, welke voor de tegenwoordige taal als stamwoord gelden, (bijv. bolau, spin), steeds op de vóór-laatste lettergreep. Op de laatste lettergreep valt de klemtoon bij alle afleidingen van één-lettergrepige stamwoorden, (welke als zoodanig niet altijd in de tegenwoordige taal meer gangbaar behoeven te zijn), of bij zulke samenstellingen, waarvan een één-lettergrepig woord het laatste lid uitmaakt, als: peta-bá, wiens long (bak) gezwollen (petak) is, = verwaand; lima-lè, zijne handteekening zetten, uit lima(k), hand, en lèk, spoor, enz.
world_status: statement found in a copy we already had

new_statements.quote: § 4. Het accent, dat in het Rottineesch duidelijk hoorbaar is, valt bij een tweelettergrepig stamwoord of bij de afleidingen daarvan, als ook op de drielettergrepige, welke voor de tegenwoordige taal als stamwoord gelden, (bijv. bolau, spin), steeds op de vóór-laatste lettergreep. Op de laatste lettergreep valt de klemtoon bij alle afleidingen van één-lettergrepige stamwoorden, [...] of bij zulke samenstellingen, waarvan een één-lettergrepig woord het laatste lid uitmaakt [...] Tevens is echter in 't oog te houden, dat de vocaal hierbij altijd gerekt is [...] [p. 6:] Verspringing van den klemtoon komt in het Rottineesch in de tegenwoordige taal niet voor.
new_statements.translation: Sec. 4. The accent, which is clearly audible in Rotinese, falls in a disyllabic stem word or in its derivatives, as also in the trisyllabic words that count as stems for the present-day language (e.g. bolau 'spider'), always on the penultimate syllable. The stress falls on the last syllable in all derivatives of monosyllabic stems [...] or in such compounds of which a monosyllabic word forms the last member [...] It must also be kept in mind that the vowel is then always lengthened [...] [p. 6:] Shifting of the stress does not occur in present-day Rotinese.
new_statements.citation: Jonker, J. C. G. 1915. Rottineesche Spraakkunst. Leiden: E. J. Brill.
new_statements.locator: Eerste Deel 'Klanken, Klemtoon, Schrift', sec. 4 'De Klemtoon', printed pp. 5-6 (Delpher scan pp. 33-34)

Eigenlijke woord-vormende suffixen ontbreken en de pronominale aanhechtsels, enz., hebben hier deze werking niet.' at line 357 (SCANPAGE 34). new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word accent is fixed on the penultimate syllable of stems (di- and trisyllabic) and their derivatives. Apparent final accent occurs only when the last member is a monosyllabic root (derivative or compound), whose vowel is always long, plus a few lexicalised words (palák 'old', kaifú, kelumèk); Edwards 2021 reanalyses these as final double vowels /VV/, making the rule 'stress the penultimate vowel' exceptionless. Accent never shifts: there are no true word-forming suffixes and pronominal attachments do not attract or move it.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Jonker sec. 4 (p. 5): words of more than three syllables (or trisyllables with final accent), whether stems or compounds, have a double accent - the strongest on the penult (or final), a weaker one on the fourth (or third) syllable from the end (luü-eik: secondary on lu; kelumèk: on ke); a monosyllabic first member of a compound keeps relative length under the secondary accent; still-living prefixes (and be, beke) never take secondary accent (p. 6). Edwards 2021:12, 35: 'Secondary stress is assigned to every second syllable to the left.'
new_statements.exceptions: Final accent in derivatives of monosyllabic roots and compounds ending in a monosyllabic root (peta-bá, lima-lè), always with a lengthened vowel; a few di-/trisyllabic words now felt as roots with final accent (palák, kaifú, kaifòk, kelumèk); reduplicated final portions stay a unit so the secondary accent sits further from the main accent (kaki-uüle, kai-lií); prefixes felt as such never bear secondary accent (napadeik, nangatuk accented only on de, tuk); in loans an epenthetic vowel can move the accent onto the new penult (holomata < hormat, p. 8).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent of stems and derived/compound words in the Termanu dialect; sec. 2 states the long-accented/short-unaccented vowel pattern holds for words in isolation or in pausa as well as in connected speech and composition; accent does not shift when short pronominal forms are attached (sec. 4 p. 6 and the Aanm. in the pronoun chapter). Jonker adds the caveat (p. 6 Aanm.) that the topic can only be treated 'in general', by ear.
new_statements.identity_note: Jonker 1915 is a grammar of 'Rottineesch' that by its own Inleiding 'behandelt in hoofdzaak den tongval van Termanoe' (treats chiefly the Termanu/Pada dialect, = Glottolog term1237), with other Rote dialects discussed alongside; the accent rule in sec. 4 is stated for Rotinese generally with Termanu forms. Edwards 2021 sec. 1.4.1.2 states the stress facts explicitly 'in Termanu'; his sec. 2.4.1 restates them for all Rote languages.

new_statements.quote: 2.3 Word stress. Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the root. The first vowel of vowel sequences carries the stress. Stress shifts to the right with the addition of syllabic object enclitics. In compounding of nouns and verbs, and in reduplication, it is the penultimate syllable of the final lexical root that bears primary word stress [' = secondary stress]. (1) ['rafu] 'ashes', ['lima-k] 'hand/arm' (2) ['oe] 'water', ['hai] 'stop, come to an end', ['tau-k] 'man' (3) ['tutu] 'pound', [tu'tuu-k] 'seat' (from root tuu- 'sit') (4) ['ina(-k)] 'mother', ['ina-g] 'my mother', [,ina-g-'ala] 'my mothers' (5) [,tasi 'oe] 'sea-water'. [sec. 2.2:] High and mid vowels have lax allophones in unstressed closed syllables.
new_statements.citation: Fox, James J. & Charles E. Grimes. 1995. Roti. In Darrell T. Tryon (ed.), Comparative Austronesian Dictionary: An Introduction to Austronesian Studies, Part 1 Fascicle 1, 611-622. Berlin/New York: Mouton de Gruyter.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing Jonker 1915 statement (penultimate on the root; Jonker's 'final stress on derivatives/compounds ending in a monosyllabic root with a long vowel' is the same thing once a long vowel counts as two nuclei, as Fox & Grimes say). Adds: first vowel of a sequence stressed, secondary stress on earlier roots, rightward shift under syllabic object enclitics. The enclitic point differs from Jonker, who writes that stress shift does not occur and that pronominal suffixes do not shift it.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the root; a vowel sequence counts as two syllables and its first vowel takes the stress (geminate vowels are two nuclei, so 'tuu-k' stresses the first 'u'); syllabic object enclitics pull stress rightward; in compounds and reduplications the final lexical root's penult carries primary stress, earlier roots carry secondary stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Marked in examples ([,ina-g-'ala] 'my mothers', [,tasi 'oe] 'sea-water'): the non-final root of a compound or the root before a stressed enclitic group carries secondary stress; no general rule stated.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress shifts right when a syllabic object enclitic is added; in compounds and reduplication only the final lexical root's penult has primary stress. The scanned of the example brackets is imperfect (some stress marks garbled), the prose is clean.
new_statements.identity_note: Fox & Grimes 1995 describe 'Rotinese' as a dialect chain (eight dialects after Jonker 1913) and say the early studies and Jonker's grammar and dictionary, as well as Fox's own work, are based on the Termanu dialect; their consonant table is stated for the Termanu dialect. Kumanireng et al. 1998 group the island into four dialects and take dialek Rote Tengah (Central Rote, the group containing Termanu and Ba'a) as their base, so both works describe the Termanu-area variety that term1237 covers.

new_statements.quote: Ciri suprasegmental yang dimaksudkan adalah tekanan kata, durasi, dan lagu kalimat [...] Semua kata, secara tersendiri, memperoleh tekanan dan tekanan pada kata (bersama dengan durasi) berperan sebagai pembeda makna. Pada kata bersuku kata dua atau lebih, tekanan diberikan pada suku penultima. Contoh: péla 'malas', náne 'berenang' (bersuku dua); kokótok 'burik', solángga (bersuku tiga); ti?ilángga 'topi', hatahóli 'manusia' (bersuku empat). Dalam konstruksi morfologis, seperti pengulangan, pengimbuhan dan pemajemukan (reduplikasi, afikasi, dan komposisi) tekanan kata selalu berada pada suku penultima kata. [p. 26:] Durasi atau perpanjangan di dalam Rote bersifat fonemis karena membedakan makna kata.
new_statements.translation: The suprasegmental features meant are word stress, duration, and sentence melody [...] Every word, taken on its own, receives stress, and stress on the word (together with duration) serves to distinguish meaning. In words of two or more syllables, stress is given to the penultimate syllable. Examples: péla 'lazy', náne 'swim' (disyllabic); kokótok 'speckled', solángga (trisyllabic); ti?ilángga 'hat', hatahóli 'human being' (four syllables). In morphological constructions such as repetition, affixation and compounding (reduplication, affixation and composition) word stress is always on the penultimate syllable of the word. [p. 26:] Duration or lengthening in Rote is phonemic because it distinguishes word meaning.
new_statements.citation: Kumanireng, Threes Y., Yosep B. Kroon, Soleman D. Taka & A. M. Fanggidae. 1998. Morfologi bahasa Rote. Jakarta: Pusat Pembinaan dan Pengembangan Bahasa.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as Jonker 1915 (penultimate). Kumanireng et al. state penultimate stress for derived and compound words as well, whereas Jonker gives final stress on derivatives/compounds whose last member is a monosyllabic (long-vowel) root; Kumanireng's own long-vowel examples (do:, te:te) are written as single syllables, so that difference is a syllable-counting convention rather than a different rule. Adds phonemic vowel length. Describes the Central Rote dialect (dialek Rote Tengah), which the authors take as the standard.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress on the penultimate syllable of every word of two or more syllables, and still on the penult of the whole word in reduplicated, affixed and compound forms (examples: horo > hohoro > makahororo; deta > dedetak > makadedetak). Vowel length is separately phonemic (do vs. do:, tete vs. te:te); the authors say stress and duration operate together and claim a meaning-distinguishing role for them, but every minimal pair they give is a length pair, not a stress-placement pair. Sentence-level accent and intonation are described separately (pp. 26-27).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for placement. Caveat: the statement 'tekanan.. (bersama dengan durasi) berperan sebagai pembeda makna' and 'in a stressed word no lengthening occurs, in an unstressed word there is lengthening' (p. 26) mix stress with phonemic vowel length; the placement rule itself is exceptionless penultimate.
new_statements.identity_note: Fox & Grimes 1995 describe 'Rotinese' as a dialect chain (eight dialects after Jonker 1913) and say the early studies and Jonker's grammar and dictionary, as well as Fox's own work, are based on the Termanu dialect; their consonant table is stated for the Termanu dialect. Kumanireng et al. 1998 group the island into four dialects and take dialek Rote Tengah (Central Rote, the group containing Termanu and Ba'a) as their base, so both works describe the Termanu-area variety that term1237 covers.

readall_conflicts: All three sources (Jonker 1915 already on record, Fox & Grimes 1995, Kumanireng et al. 1998) put primary stress on the penultimate syllable, so placement is not in dispute. Two second-order disagreements: (a) clitics - Jonker 1915 p. 6 says stress shift does not occur in the modern language and that pronominal suffixes do not cause it, while Fox & Grimes 1995 p. 614 say stress shifts to the right when a syllabic object enclitic is added (their [,ina-g-'ala] 'my mothers'); Jonker's suffix examples are the non-syllabic -n/-s, so the two may be describing different clitics, but they are stated as opposites. (b) derived/compound words - Jonker and Fox & Grimes give final stress on forms ending in a monosyllabic long-vowel root (= penult of the final root once a long vowel counts as two nuclei), whereas Kumanireng et al. say stress in reduplicated, affixed and compound words is always on the penult of the whole word; their examples (hohoro, makahororo, dedetak) do not involve final long-vowel roots, so the statements do not meet. Kumanireng et al.'s claim that stress together with duration distinguishes meaning is a statement about phonemic vowel length, not about contrastive stress placement.

sources.locator: printed p. 614, section 2.3 Word stress; examples (4)-(5) printed p. 615
sources.note: Penultimate primary stress on the root confirms the catalog's fixed penultimate rule (cite Jonker 1915). Added detail: geminate vowels count as two syllabic nuclei and the first vowel of a vowel sequence takes the stress ([tu'tuu-k], ['tau-k], ['hai]); stress shifts right when syllabic object enclitics are added ([ˋina-ŋ-'ala]); in compounds and reduplication the final lexical root carries primary stress and the earlier root a secondary ([ˋtasi 'oe]). Secondary stress is stated morphologically (non-final root), not as an alternating count; the two four-syllable examples fit the catalog's 1010

Secondary stress is assigned to every second syllable to the left.' and 'Given that stress falls on the penultimate vowel of a word, a double vowel will always contain a vowel that is the locus of stress'; Jonker's final-accented forms (nadá, na-tafú) reanalysed as final double vowels /aa/, /uu/. tone.quote: Both Middelkoop (1972) and Jonker (1908) transcribe sequences of two identical vowels with a single orthographic letter. In Jonker (1908), such double vowels are also marked with an acute or grave accent in certain cases according to the quality of the vowel and the placement of stress.
